lesson.title: Compressing Huge Ratios: The Logic Behind the Decibel
lesson.summary: The decibel turns unwieldy power ratios into a compact logarithmic scale, so that a million to one difference in power becomes a manageable 60 dB instead of a number with six zeros.
lesson.body:
The decibel, abbreviated dB, is a logarithmic unit used to express the ratio between two power levels: dB = 10 times log base 10 of (P2/P1), where P2 and P1 are the two powers being compared. Because it is built on a logarithm, the decibel scale compresses enormous ratios into small, manageable numbers. A power ratio of 1,000,000 to 1 becomes just 60 dB, since 10 times log10(1,000,000) = 10 times 6 = 60, while a raw ratio like a million to one is awkward to write, compare, or add up across a chain of amplifier stages.

Because electrical power is related to voltage by P = V^2/R, a decibel expressed in terms of voltage picks up a factor of 2 out front instead of 10: dB = 20 times log10(V2/V1), but only when V1 and V2 are measured across the same resistance, so that the R cancels out of the ratio consistently. This is why the decibel is defined starting from power rather than voltage or current: power is the quantity where the base definition, 10 log10 of a ratio, is unambiguous, and the voltage and current versions are just consequences of that squared relationship, valid only under the equal impedance assumption.

An amplifier receives an input power of 2 mW and delivers an output power of 200 mW. Its power gain in decibels is 10 times log10(P_out/P_in) = 10 times log10(200/2) = 10 times log10(100). Since log10(100) = 2 exactly, because 10^2 = 100, the gain is 10 times 2 = 20 dB.

The same amplifier, if it happens to have equal input and output impedance, would show a voltage gain factor of exactly 10, since power scales as voltage squared and the power ratio was 100. Checking with the voltage formula: dB = 20 times log10(10) = 20 times 1 = 20 dB, since log10(10) = 1 exactly, matching the 20 dB found from power directly. Two handy rules of thumb fall straight out of this: doubling power adds 10 times log10(2) = 3.01 dB, so roughly 3 dB, and a tenfold increase in power adds exactly 10 dB, which is why doubling twice, a factor of 4, adds about 6 dB, and why the earlier 100 times power ratio, two factors of ten, landed on exactly 20 dB.

A negative decibel value simply signals attenuation rather than gain: a filter that cuts power in half, from P1 down to P1/2, produces dB = 10 log10(0.5) = -3.01 dB, the well known 3 dB point used to define a filter's cutoff frequency, the spot where output power has dropped to exactly half the input power. Zero dB itself means no change at all, P2 = P1, since log10(1) = 0.

Decibels are additive precisely because logarithms turn multiplication into addition, so a signal chain of three amplifier stages with gains of 20 dB, 15 dB, and 10 dB has a combined gain of 20 + 15 + 10 = 45 dB, found by simple addition instead of multiplying three separate gain factors together and then converting the messy product back into a ratio. That additive property, more than the compression of large numbers, is the real reason decibels dominate audio engineering, RF design, and filter specifications.
